originalTitle: The clock is running out for America’s most contentious spying law
summary: Weeks before the end of the legislative session, some members of Congress are scrambling to reauthorize a controversial warrantless wiretapping authority, possibly by attaching it to a must-pass military spending bill. content: Weeks before the end of the legislative session, some members of Congress are scrambling to reauthorize a controversial warrantless wiretapping authority, possibly by attaching it to a must-pass military spending bill. Sen. Mike Rounds (R-SD) told Politico that Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) could be attached to the National Defense Authorization Act. It’s the latest in a grueling fight over a major spying rule that hasn’t technically lapsed. “We don’t have two weeks to work just on FISA,” said Rounds, a member of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence. “But if it’s amended onto the NDAA then you can move it forward and get that done in time.” FISA allows for the warrantless surveillance of certain foreigners’ communications, ostensibly on national security grounds. In part because of FISA’s broad scope, Congress revisits it every few years, both to reauthorize the authority and to reform it. The last effort to do both failed. Despite pressure from President Donald Trump, Congress failed to reauthorize FISA over the summer, in part because leadership wouldn’t allow any amendments — particularly attempts to limit its sweeping scope — to be debated or introduced. (Trump didn’t help matters when he made Bill Pulte the acting director of national intelligence. Pulte, who reportedly bragged about purging one-third of the DNI staff, is now the director of federal housing.) But the surveillance authority didn’t actually lapse because the FISA court rectified surveillance under Section 702 back in March, meaning the surveillance state can keep chugging along as is for another four months. So why the urgency? If you haven’t heard, there’s about to be a new Congress in town — one that is even less likely to give Trump seemingly unlimited spying powers without some semblance of reform. Support for — and opposition to — FISA isn’t a clear-cut partisan issue. Last time around, a bipartisan coalition led by House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) and Rep. Jim Himes (D-CT), the ranking member of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, led the campaign for a “clean” reauthorization of FISA. Their efforts were defeated largely because of holdouts from the Freedom Caucus, whose privacy concerns echoed those of liberal lawmakers. FISA’s critics wanted reform, not abolition. Their goal was to make it harder for intelligence agencies to use the statute, which is intended for foreign targets, to access Americans’ communications. “It was remarkable watching two dozen House Republicans stand up to the establishment, stand up to Mike Johnson, and fight to reform FISA,” said Michael Baick, an organizer with the OpenAI boycott campaign QuitGPT, which has been advocating for FISA reform to stop AI surveillance. “This has always been a bipartisan issue where Americans of all stripes can agree, and trying to make deals with the establishment to maintain the status quo, while the ground is shifting, is just short-sighted and missing what this moment really is.” Johnson and Himes were adamantly opposed to any reining in of Section 702, stressing the need for a so-called “clean reauthorization.” Both claimed there had already been reforms. “It ain’t the same FISA,” Rep. Jim Jordan (R-OH) declared in April. But the changes reformers most wanted were missing. Among them were a warrant requirement and an end to what critics say are major loopholes. Under Section 702, intelligence agencies can pull the communications of non-US persons not in the United States — that is, foreign nationals outside the country. But federal agencies like the FBI and NSA can buy Americans’ data from private brokers, a practice FBI director Kash Patel admits is ongoing. And intelligence agencies can use Section 702 to obtain the communications of non-US persons who are communicating with Americans — a workaround known as the “backdoor search loophole.” “I think it’s a Hail Mary by surveillance hawks to try to ram through what they wanted to do the entire time,” Don Bell, senior policy counsel at the Constitution Project of the Project on Government Oversight, told The Verge. “This is something everyone knew was coming down the pike. There have been months to do this, and I don’t think anyone is saying don’t reauthorize at all. The argument is this is an incredibly powerful surveillance tool, and there needs to be guardrails in place to protect people’s constitutional rights.” Himes, arguably the Democratic Party’s biggest champion of FISA, seems willing to give Trump one more win before the blue wave crashes down in Washington. “I made it clear to some very senior administration officials that they should get this thing done in the lame-duck,” he told The Hill, “because it’s, you know, going to be a very different 702 that gets reauthorized in the first quarter of next year.” But Himes didn’t have the votes this summer, and it’s even less likely that he’ll have the votes for a clean reauthorization now.
chineseTitle: 美国最具争议的间谍法已经时日不多了
chineseSummary: 在立法会议结束前几周，一些国会议员正忙于重新授权一项有争议的无证窃听机构，可能是将其附加到一项必须通过的军费开支法案中。参议员迈克·朗兹 (R-SD) 告诉 Politico，《外国情报监视法》(FISA) 第 702 条可以附加到国防授权中 [...]
chineseContent: 在立法会议结束前几周，一些国会议员正忙于重新授权一项有争议的无证窃听机构，可能是将其附加到一项必须通过的军费开支法案中。参议员迈克·朗兹 (R-SD) 告诉 Politico，《外国情报监视法》(FISA) 第 702 条可以附加到《国防授权法》中。这是围绕一项主要间谍规则展开的艰苦斗争中的最新一起，该规则在技术上尚未失效。参议院情报特别委员会成员朗兹表示：“我们没有两周的时间来处理 FISA 问题。” “但如果它被修改到 NDAA 中，那么你就可以向前推进并及时完成。” FISA 允许在没有授权的情况下监视某些外国人的通信，表面上是出于国家安全的考虑。部分原因是 FISA 的范围广泛，国会每隔几年就会重新审议一次，既是为了重新授权该机构，也是为了对其进行改革。最后的努力都失败了。尽管面临唐纳德·特朗普总统的压力，国会还是未能在今年夏天重新授权《外国情报监视法案》，部分原因是领导层不允许任何修正案——特别是试图限制其广泛范围的修正案——进行辩论或提出。 （特朗普任命比尔·普尔特（Bill Pulte）为代理国家情报总监，这对事情没有任何帮助。据报道，普尔特吹嘘清洗了三分之一的国家情报局工作人员，现在是联邦住房局局长。）但监视权实际上并没有失效，因为 FISA 法院早在 3 月份就根据第 702 条纠正了监视行为，这意味着监视国家可以继续正常运转四个月。那么为什么这么紧迫呢？如果你还没有听说过，城里即将召开新一届国会——新一届国会不太可能给予特朗普看似无限的间谍活动
